provenance: Authored from EkagraAI Final Course Content Ground Truth (C1–C4), version 1.0, and the approved C3.1 and C3.2 design discussions. C3.x.Oxx identifiers are locally assigned references mapped to the ordered content requirements of the corresponding Ground Truth subsection; they are not official identifiers from the source document. This contract records instructional design only; it does not certify implementation or experimental effectiveness. V1.2 is a targeted pedagogy/guard/causal-integration revision; locked scientific content and authored move IDs remain unchanged.

control_boundary.backend: active move, verified material, completion ledger and progression
control_boundary.frontend: optional passive visuals; never model generated
control_boundary.tutor: natural explanation, learner contingencies and doubts within authored move
control_boundary.judge: learner-visible delivery evidence and pedagogy fidelity, never mastery

shared_guards: Visual display alone is not delivery evidence
A learner doubt can interrupt a move without changing its position
The receiver is not presumed to possess the uncorrupted original frame
Distinguish original data cells from transmitted checking-bit cells whenever positions are discussed
Parity checks apply to complete checked groups, including checking-bit cells and the bottom-right corner bit
A passing check is not proof that transmission was error-free
For an initially valid checking group, an odd number of flips reverses its parity result and an even number leaves it unchanged
Apply the odd/even flip relationship independently to each complete row and column
Distinguish the instructor's knowledge of a constructed transmission history from the receiver's available evidence
Do not claim that one failed row and one failed column prove exactly one bit changed
Do not claim unique localization or successful correction without the required error-count assumption

P2 requires one genuine learner response opportunity per guided move and accurate Tutor follow-through; hints are contingent on need, a wrong or uncertain response never creates a mastery gate, and an extra confirmation answer is never mandatory
Do not infer mastery or SOLO level from move completion or a correct response
C3.1 explains how changed positions produce checking outcomes; C3.2 interprets what observed outcomes do and do not establish
Do not introduce unfamiliar non-grid checking arrangements or formal coding theory; those are outside C3

C3.1.position_notation: RrCc, with rows and columns numbered from 1
C3.1.initial_state: All seven complete checking groups pass even parity.
C3.1.general_relationship: For an initially valid checking group, an odd number of flips within that group reverses its original parity result; an even number leaves its original result unchanged. Apply this independently to each complete row and column.

position_roles.coordinate_rule: RrCc is 1-based; R1–R2 are the original two data rows and C1–C3 are the original three data columns.
position_roles.transmitted_cells: All 12 positions are transmitted and subject to possible bit flips; every position belongs to exactly one complete row and one complete column.

C3.2.position_notation: RrCc, with rows and columns numbered from 1
C3.2.receiver_evidence: The received complete grid and the agreed even-parity checking rules/results; the uncorrupted original transmission is not presumed available.

case_D_same_received_grid_one_flip_histo.name: one_flip_history_for_ambiguous_received_grid
case_D_same_received_grid_one_flip_histo.original_grid_validity: All seven complete row and column groups pass even parity.
case_D_same_received_grid_one_flip_histo.learner_facing_label: one-flip history for the ambiguous received grid

case_E_same_received_grid_three_flip_his.name: three_flip_history_for_same_ambiguous_received_grid
case_E_same_received_grid_three_flip_his.original_grid_validity: All seven complete row and column groups pass even parity.
case_E_same_received_grid_three_flip_his.receiver_inference: The receiver observes the same complete received grid and the same seven check results under either history; the actual history and error count cannot be distinguished from these observations alone.
case_E_same_received_grid_three_flip_his.learner_facing_label: three-flip history for the same received grid

case_F_four_corner_rectangle.name: four_flipped_data_bits_at_rectangle_corners
case_F_four_corner_rectangle.receiver_inference: No parity violation is detected; this does not establish that no transmitted bits changed.

interpretive_rules: Different valid original grids and different transmission histories can produce the same received grid and identical checking results.
A one-failed-row/one-failed-column pattern is consistent with a single flipped bit at the intersection, but does not prove the exactly-one-error assumption.
A multi-bit pattern can imitate the checking result of a one-bit pattern; correction under an assumed one-error case may therefore be unjustified.
A four-corner rectangle can contain two flips in each affected row and column, leaving all seven checks passing.
A failed check detects a violated rule; a passing check means that rule is satisfied. Passing all checks does not prove an error-free transmission.

position_roles.coordinate_rule: RrCc is 1-based; R1–R2 are the original two data rows and C1–C3 are the original three data columns.
position_roles.transmitted_cells: All 12 positions are transmitted and subject to possible bit flips; every position belongs to exactly one complete row and one complete column.

C3.1.title: Understanding the Relationships Behind Checking Results
C3.1.section_objective: Develop an integrated causal explanation of how changed bit positions, checking-group membership and combined flip effects produce observed row and column pass/fail results.

content_reference_legend.C3.1.O01: How changing one transmitted bit affects every check that includes that bit.
content_reference_legend.C3.1.O02: How multiple flipped bits combine within a given check.
content_reference_legend.C3.1.O03: Why an odd number of flips reverses a check result while an even number leaves it unchanged, relative to an initially valid group.
content_reference_legend.C3.1.O04: How positions and combinations of changes determine which familiar row and column checks pass or fail.
content_reference_legend.C3.1.O05: Connect these causal relationships to the single- and two-dimensional parity properties learned in C2.
content_reference_legend.C3.1.O06: Reason from an error pattern to checking results, explaining why observations arise rather than memorizing outcomes.

P1.source_instructional_action: Introduce the valid 3-by-4 grid and its seven even-parity checks; distinguish data from checking cells, then explain how the bit in row 1, column 2 and the corner bit each belong to one complete row and column check.
P1.exact_delivery:
Look at the grid. It has three rows and four columns.

The first three cells of rows 1 and 2 are data bits. The rightmost column and bottom row contain checking bits, including the corner. All three rows and four columns pass their even-parity checks.

Every bit belongs to a row and a column check. The bit in row 1, column 2 belongs to both those checks. The corner bit in row 3, column 4 belongs to row 3 and column 4.
P1.completion_evidence: Tutor establishes the initially valid 3-by-4 grid and seven passing checks; distinguishes data cells, row-checking cells, column-checking cells and the corner; explains that the bit in row 1, column 2 belongs to row 1 and column 2, while the corner in row 3, column 4 belongs to row 3 and column 4.

P1.source_instructional_action: Model the two verified single-flip cases with the visible grids; explain why each flip fails its two containing checks and contrast a data cell with the corner checking cell, without inferring a unique error from checks alone.
P1.exact_delivery:
In the first grid, the bit in row 1, column 2 changes from 0 to 1. Row 1 and column 2 now fail because both contain that bit.

In the second grid, the corner checking bit in row 3, column 4 changes from 1 to 0. This time, row 3 and column 4 fail. The other five checks pass in each example.

A change to a data bit or a checking bit affects the row and column that contain it.
P1.completion_evidence: Tutor correctly identifies both single-bit changes (row 1, column 2 and row 3, column 4), their distinct failed checks (row 1 and column 2 versus row 3 and column 4), and why membership explains the outcomes; does not claim that check results alone prove a unique error location.

P1.source_instructional_action: Work the verified two-changes-in-one-row example shown on the grid. Explain why the shared row still passes but the two affected columns fail, counting changes separately inside each check.
P1.exact_delivery:
Two bits change in row 1: one in column 1 and one in column 2.

Row 1 contains two changes, so its check still passes. But columns 1 and 2 each contain one change, so both checks fail. All other checks pass.

We must count the changes in each row and column separately.
P1.completion_evidence: Tutor identifies row 1, column 1 and row 1, column 2, explains that row 1 passes because it contains two flips while column 1 and column 2 fail because each contains one, and distinguishes within-group flip counts from the total error count.

P1.source_instructional_action: Compare the two verified grids: first, two changes in column 1 leave column 1 passing while rows 1 and 2 fail; next, two changes in different rows and columns make four checks fail. Explain how positions change the outcome.
P1.exact_delivery:
Both grids have two changed bits.

In the first, a bit changes in row 1, column 1 and another in row 2, column 1. Column 1 has two changes and still passes. Rows 1 and 2 each have one change, so both fail.

In the second, the bits change in row 1, column 1 and row 2, column 2. Now rows 1 and 2 and columns 1 and 2 all fail: each contains one change.

The number of changes is the same. Their positions make the difference.
P1.completion_evidence: Tutor correctly contrasts the first example (rows 1 and 2 FAIL, column 1 PASS) with the second (rows 1 and 2 and columns 1 and 2 FAIL); explains that each check contains one or two changes and that position, not the total number of changes alone, determines the result.

P1.source_instructional_action: Consolidate the causal rule in plain language: one flip reverses a containing check; two flips within that check restore its passing result, not its bit values. Connect single parity with overlapping complete row and column checks of full 2D parity.
P1.exact_delivery:
A changed bit affects the row and column checks that contain it. One change makes an initially passing check fail; a second change within that same check makes it pass again. The bits have still changed.

So an odd number of changes within a check makes it fail, while an even number leaves it passing—provided the check was valid to begin with.

Single parity uses one complete check. Two-dimensional parity applies the same rule to overlapping rows and columns, including checking bits.
P1.completion_evidence: Tutor explains toggle-then-toggle-back, initial validity, odd/even flips within each complete group, the connection between single parity and overlapping full-2D row/column checks, and the positions→membership→flip count→outcomes relationship without re-listing all five cases.

P2.source_instructional_action: Introduce the valid grid and checking-bit roles. Highlight the target data bit and ask which row and column contain it without stating its coordinates beforehand. After the response, identify the highlighted bit and the corner bit by their numbered row and column; offer a hint only if useful.
P2.exact_delivery:
SHOW: This valid grid has data bits in the first three cells of rows 1 and 2. The right and bottom edges contain checking bits. All seven row and column checks pass. Highlight one data bit, but do not name its position yet.

ASK ONCE: Which row and column checks contain the highlighted bit?

HINT IF NEEDED: Look at the row and column labels beside that bit.

AFTER RESPONSE: The highlighted bit is in row 1, column 2, so it belongs to both checks. The corner checking bit is in row 3, column 4 and belongs to those two checks. Continue regardless of the answer.
P2.completion_evidence: One genuine response opportunity about the highlighted bit without revealing its position in the question; after the reply, Tutor explains that the bit lies in row 1, column 2 and the corner lies in row 3, column 4, and distinguishes data from checking cells. No correctness gate.

P2.source_instructional_action: Show the one-data-bit-change example first with results hidden; ask one focused prediction question. After the learner replies, explain its results and the corner-checking-bit comparison without another required question.
P2.exact_delivery:
SHOW FIRST: One highlighted data bit changes from 0 to 1. Hide the check results and the second example.

ASK ONCE: Which row and column checks fail because this bit changed?

HINT IF NEEDED: Find the row and column containing the highlighted bit.

AFTER RESPONSE: The change is in row 1, column 2. Both those checks fail because they contain it; the other five pass.

THEN SHOW: The corner checking bit in row 3, column 4 changes from 1 to 0. Row 3 and column 4 fail for the same reason. Continue without another required question.
P2.completion_evidence: One response opportunity about Case A before revealing its results; accurate explanation that A fails row 1 and column 2 and B fails row 3 and column 4, both from group membership, with no second compulsory question or early answer reveal.

P2.source_instructional_action: Show the same-row two-change example with outcomes hidden; ask one question about the results for row 1 and columns 1 and 2. Explain the within-check change counts after the response.
P2.exact_delivery:
SHOW: Two highlighted bits change in row 1, in columns 1 and 2. Keep the check results hidden.

ASK ONCE: Which checks pass or fail for row 1 and columns 1 and 2?

HINT IF NEEDED: Count changes inside each row or column separately.

AFTER RESPONSE: Row 1 has two changes, so it still passes. Columns 1 and 2 each have one change, so both fail. All other checks pass. Continue regardless of the answer.
P2.completion_evidence: One genuine prediction opportunity; Tutor correctly explains row 1 PASS and column 1 and column 2 FAIL via within-group counts, with optional hint and correct follow-through even after an incorrect response.

P2.source_instructional_action: Show only the same-column two-change example before the learner responds; ask whether column 1 passes. Then explain that column 1 passes while rows 1 and 2 fail, and contrast it with the different-row-and-column example without another compulsory question.
P2.exact_delivery:
SHOW FIRST: Two bits change in column 1, one in row 1 and one in row 2. Hide the results and second example.

ASK ONCE: Does column 1 pass or fail after these two changes?

HINT IF NEEDED: Count the changes inside column 1.

AFTER RESPONSE: Column 1 has two changes and still passes. Rows 1 and 2 each have one change, so both fail.

THEN COMPARE: In the second grid, one bit changes in row 1, column 1 and another in row 2, column 2. Each of rows 1 and 2 and columns 1 and 2 contains one change, so all four fail. Continue without another required question.
P2.completion_evidence: One response opportunity about whether column 1 passes in the first example; Tutor correctly explains that column 1 passes while rows 1 and 2 fail, then contrasts the second example with four failed checks and the corresponding within-check counts. No premature second example or extra compulsory question.

P2.source_instructional_action: Ask for one integrated causal explanation of check outcomes; supply the complete initial-validity/odd-even/toggling rule and single-to-2D bridge regardless of answer, without a mastery quiz.
P2.exact_delivery:
ASK ONCE: After some bits change, what decides whether a row or column check passes or fails?

HINT IF NEEDED: Look at which bits belong to that check, then count how many changed.

AFTER RESPONSE: Every change affects the checks containing that bit. Starting from a valid check, one change makes it fail; two changes within it leave it passing. More generally, odd numbers of changes make it fail and even numbers leave it passing. Single parity checks one complete group; two-dimensional parity applies the same rule to overlapping rows and columns, including checking bits. Continue regardless of the answer.
P2.completion_evidence: One causal-reasoning response opportunity and responsive Tutor explanation of initial validity, toggle/cancellation, odd/even counts in each complete group, and the single-to-full-2D bridge; no correctness gate or extra confirmation question.

P3.source_instructional_action: Compare the initially valid grid with the one-data-bit-change grid. Keep the parity rules fixed; explain why the one changed bit affects only its complete row and column.
P3.exact_delivery:
Compare the valid grid with the one beside it. Both use the same even-parity rule.

In the first, every row and column passes. In the second, only the bit in row 1, column 2 changes from 0 to 1. Row 1 and column 2 fail because both contain it; the other five checks pass.

The rule is unchanged. The changed position explains the different results.
P3.completion_evidence: Tutor compares valid grid and A, states the unchanged check rules, single data-bit change at row 1, column 2, row 1 and column 2 failures and other passes, and explains the group-membership difference.

P3.source_instructional_action: Compare the two one-flip cases, holding the even-parity rules and number of flips fixed; explain why changing a data bit versus the corner checking bit changes which checks fail.
P3.exact_delivery:
Both examples use the same even-parity rule, and each has exactly one changed bit.

In the first, a data bit in row 1, column 2 changes, so row 1 and column 2 fail. In the second, the corner checking bit in row 3, column 4 changes, so row 3 and column 4 fail. The other checks pass in both.

The number of changes stays the same. Different positions affect different checks—even when a checking bit changes.
P3.completion_evidence: Tutor contrasts A and B with one-flip count and parity rules held fixed, identifies data versus corner checking position, and correctly links row 1 and column 2 versus row 3 and column 4 failed checks to membership.

P3.source_instructional_action: Compare two changed bits sharing a row against two sharing a column. Explain the passing shared check and the failing individual perpendicular checks in each example.
P3.exact_delivery:
Both grids start with valid checks and have two changed bits.

In the first, both changes are in row 1. That row still passes because it has two changes; columns 1 and 2 each have one change and fail.

In the second, both changes are in column 1. Now column 1 passes, while rows 1 and 2 fail.

The total is still two changes. What differs is which check contains both.
P3.completion_evidence: Tutor compares the two-change cases. In the first, row 1 passes while columns 1 and 2 fail. In the second, column 1 passes while rows 1 and 2 fail. It explains that the total number of changes stays constant while the shared check differs.

P3.source_instructional_action: Compare two changed bits sharing a row against two placed in different rows and columns, using the same valid starting grid. Explain why the first arrangement fails two checks and the second fails four.
P3.exact_delivery:
Both examples start with the same valid grid and have two changed bits.

In the first, both changes are in row 1. That row passes, while columns 1 and 2 fail.

In the second, the changes are in row 1, column 1 and row 2, column 2. Rows 1 and 2 and columns 1 and 2 each have one change, so all four checks fail.

The same number of changes gives different results because the changes belong to different checks.
P3.completion_evidence: Tutor contrasts C versus E with two flips fixed, correctly states C's passing row 1 and failed column 1 and column 2 against E's four failed checks, and explains the group-specific distribution.

P3.source_instructional_action: Synthesize the contrasts into an explicit initial-validity, within-group odd/even explanation, contrasting one complete check for single parity with several overlapping checks in full 2D parity.
P3.exact_delivery:
Across these comparisons, the number of changed bits alone does not tell us which checks will fail. We must see which rows and columns contain them.

Starting from valid checks, one change within a check makes it fail. Two changes within that same check leave it passing, although the bits have changed. Odd numbers of changes make it fail; even numbers leave it passing.

Single parity checks one complete group. Two-dimensional parity applies that same rule to overlapping rows and columns, including checking bits.
P3.completion_evidence: Tutor uses the contrasted cases to explain positions→membership→within-group counts→outcomes, the initial-validity condition, odd/even toggling, and the one-group versus overlapping-full-2D difference without only listing outcomes.

C3.2.title: Interpreting Checking Evidence and Its Limitations
C3.2.section_objective: Interpret checking evidence using the causal model developed in C3.1, explain why ambiguous or undetected outcomes arise, and distinguish justified receiver inference from unsupported assumptions.

content_reference_legend.C3.2.O01: Reason from observed checking results to possible error patterns without assuming the original data are directly available to the receiver.
content_reference_legend.C3.2.O02: Understand that different actual error patterns can produce identical checking results.
content_reference_legend.C3.2.O03: Explain how a multi-bit pattern can imitate the checking result of one changed bit and why correction based on a presumed one-error case may be unjustified.
content_reference_legend.C3.2.O04: Explain how some multiple-error arrangements remain undetected, including the four-corner rectangle in a row/column parity grid.
content_reference_legend.C3.2.O05: Understand how the number-of-errors assumption affects justified localization and correction claims.
content_reference_legend.C3.2.O06: Integrate changed positions, affected rules, pass/fail patterns, ambiguity and limits of receiver inference into coherent explanations.

P1.source_instructional_action: Explain the receiver evidence boundary using a received 3-by-4 grid; distinguish check results from instructor-known transmission history without calling a receiver-visible grid the pristine original.
P1.exact_delivery:
Here is a complete received grid. The receiver can read all twelve bits and check its three rows and four columns using even parity.

But it cannot see a clean copy of the grid as it was sent. We may know which bits changed in a teaching example; the receiver does not automatically know that history.

A failed check means a parity rule is broken. A passing check means that rule is satisfied, not that every bit is unchanged.
P1.completion_evidence: Tutor distinguishes the received grid and agreed checking rules/results from instructor-only knowledge of the original and flips; accurately states the limited meaning of PASS and FAIL.

P1.source_instructional_action: Start with two receiver-observed check patterns; explain one possible two-bit history for each, explicitly avoiding unique-location or proven-error-count claims.
P1.exact_delivery:
First, look at the check results: every row passes, but columns 1 and 2 fail. One possible explanation is two changes in row 1, in columns 1 and 2. Row 1 would still pass, while both columns fail.

In the second grid, rows 1 and 2 and columns 1 and 2 fail. One possible explanation is a change in row 1, column 1 and another in row 2, column 2.

These arrangements fit the observations. The receiver has not proved that these exact bits—or exactly two bits—changed.
P1.completion_evidence: Tutor begins from both correct observed check patterns, provides the corresponding possible same-row and different-row/column two-bit explanations, and explicitly rejects unique-error-history or error-count certainty.

P1.source_instructional_action: Demonstrate the ambiguity using both different valid original grids, their one-bit versus three-bit changes, and the identical complete received grid; connect this to correction under an unproved assumption.
P1.exact_delivery:
This received grid fails row 2 and column 1. Does that prove one bit changed? No.

Look at the two different valid original grids shown. In the first, changing row 2, column 1 produces this received grid—one change.

In the second, changing row 1, columns 1 and 2, and row 2, column 2 produces exactly the same received grid—three changes.

The receiver sees identical bits and checks in both histories. It cannot tell which happened. Correcting the intersection is justified only if the exactly-one-error assumption is warranted.
P1.completion_evidence: Tutor accurately identifies both distinct valid original grids and their exact one- and three-flip histories, shows the identical received grid and failed row 2/column 1 results, and explains the conditional correction limit.

P1.source_instructional_action: Explain the verified four-corner rectangle as an undetected history, explicitly distinguishing instructor-known flips from all-pass evidence at the receiver.
P1.exact_delivery:
Here the instructor changes four bits: row 1, columns 1 and 2, and row 2, columns 1 and 2. They form a rectangle.

Each affected row and column contains two changes, so all four of those checks still pass. The other three checks also pass.

The receiver therefore sees all seven checks passing, even though four bits changed. Passing checks do not prove that the received grid matches what was sent.
P1.completion_evidence: Tutor identifies the four rectangle corners and two flips in each affected row/column, explains why all seven checks pass despite corruption, and states the receiver cannot infer no errors.

P1.source_instructional_action: Synthesize the limits of observed evidence in three distinct claims—detection, possible location and conditional correction—using earlier evidence without narrating every grid again.
P1.exact_delivery:
Checking results tell the receiver which parity rules pass or fail, not the exact transmission history.

A failed row and column may suggest their intersection, but our one-flip and three-flip histories show why that is not proof of one error. A four-corner rectangle shows that even seven passing checks cannot prove nothing changed.

So keep three claims separate: a failed check detects a rule violation; an error location may be only a possibility; and correction needs a justified assumption about how many bits changed.
P1.completion_evidence: Tutor integrates receiver-visible evidence, same-observation ambiguity, undetected rectangle, and separate detection/localization/correction claims without overstating what PASS/FAIL establishes.

P2.source_instructional_action: Ask one accessible question about receiver-visible evidence, then clarify received grid/rules versus unknown original, without turning the question into an assessment gate.
P2.exact_delivery:
ASK ONCE: The receiver can see a received grid. Does that tell it exactly which bits changed during transmission?
HINT IF NEEDED: Does the receiver also have an unchanged copy of what was sent?
FOLLOW THROUGH: No. The receiver has all twelve received bits and the agreed even-parity checks. It can determine which rows and columns pass or fail. It does not automatically know the original grid or which bits changed. In a teaching example, only the instructor may know that constructed history. A passing check is not proof that no change occurred.
P2.completion_evidence: One genuine question and response opportunity; Tutor responds contingently and accurately distinguishes visible received grid and checks from unavailable original/history, without requiring correctness to progress.

P2.source_instructional_action: Ask for one possible two-bit history from displayed observed results, then explain and contrast the second pattern without another required learner question.
P2.exact_delivery:
ASK ONCE: Every row passes, but columns 1 and 2 fail. What two-bit arrangement could explain those results?
HINT IF NEEDED: Think of two changes in the same row, but different columns.
FOLLOW THROUGH: One possibility is changing row 1, columns 1 and 2. Row 1 then has two changes and passes, while columns 1 and 2 each have one and fail. Compare the second observed pattern: rows 1 and 2 and columns 1 and 2 all fail. Changes at row 1, column 1 and row 2, column 2 could explain it. Neither observation proves exactly which bits or how many bits changed.
P2.completion_evidence: One answer-withheld candidate-history question based on visibly given check outcomes; contingent follow-through explains both correct examples as possible, not proven or unique, with no second compulsory question.

P2.source_instructional_action: Ask what the receiver can establish about the error count from the one-row/one-column failed observation; only after the response demonstrate both verified original histories and correction uncertainty.
P2.exact_delivery:
ASK ONCE: Row 2 and column 1 fail in this received grid. Can those results prove how many bits changed?
HINT IF NEEDED: Could different valid originals lead to the same received bits?
FOLLOW THROUGH: No. The two different valid original grids shown can both produce this same received grid. In the first, only row 2, column 1 changes. In the second, row 1, columns 1 and 2, and row 2, column 2 change. Both histories give the same received bits, with only row 2 and column 1 failing. The receiver cannot tell whether one or three bits changed. Correcting the intersection requires a justified exactly-one-error assumption.
P2.completion_evidence: One genuine observation-based question; after learner opportunity Tutor explains both valid origins, exact differing histories and identical received grid/checks, and conditional correction; hints only if needed.

P2.source_instructional_action: Ask whether observed all-pass results establish error-free transmission; after the response reveal the four-corner teacher-created history as the verified counterexample.
P2.exact_delivery:
ASK ONCE: All seven checks pass on this received grid. Does that prove the bits arrived unchanged?
HINT IF NEEDED: Could two changes in the same row leave its parity passing?
FOLLOW THROUGH: No. One possible history changes four rectangle corners: row 1, columns 1 and 2, and row 2, columns 1 and 2. Each affected row and column has two changes, so its check still passes. The other checks also pass. The receiver sees no parity violation, but the bits have changed. Passing is not proof of an unchanged transmission.
P2.completion_evidence: One genuine all-pass inference question with no pre-response rectangle reveal; Tutor subsequently explains four changed corners, two changes per affected group, all seven PASS, and limits of receiver inference.

P2.source_instructional_action: Ask one focused conditional-correction question; after response synthesize detection versus localization versus correction using the ambiguity and rectangle examples.
P2.exact_delivery:
ASK ONCE: Row 2 and column 1 fail. What must you assume before correcting the bit where they meet?
HINT IF NEEDED: Could several changes produce the same failed checks?
FOLLOW THROUGH: You would need a justified exactly-one-error assumption. The intersection is a possible changed position, not proof of the actual history; one- and three-flip histories can lead to the same received grid. A failed check detects a violated parity rule, not necessarily the exact changes. And all checks passing does not prove there were no changes, as the rectangle showed. Detection, localization and correction are different claims.
P2.completion_evidence: One conditional correction question and contingent explanation of single-error assumption, ambiguous histories, undetected rectangle, and distinction among detection/localization/correction.

P3.source_instructional_action: Contrast teacher-known constructed history and receiver-only observation for the same kind of received grid; make their information difference the explicit point of contrast.
P3.exact_delivery:
Consider two views of one received grid.

The instructor knows the original bits and which positions were changed to create the example. The receiver sees only the received bits and the agreed parity rules. It can check all three rows and four columns, but it cannot compare them with an unseen original.

The difference matters: the instructor can describe what happened in the constructed example; the receiver can only say what might have happened. A failed check shows a broken rule. Passing checks do not prove the transmission was unchanged.
P3.completion_evidence: Tutor explicitly contrasts teacher-known original/changes against receiver-visible grid/rules/results and distinguishes demonstrated history from warranted receiver inference.

P3.source_instructional_action: Contrast two receiver-visible failure patterns before presenting illustrative two-bit explanations; preserve the pattern-to-possible-history direction.
P3.exact_delivery:
Compare these two received grids.

In the first, every row passes but columns 1 and 2 fail. Two changes in row 1, columns 1 and 2, could explain this: the row has two changes, but each column has one.

In the second, rows 1 and 2 and columns 1 and 2 fail. Changes in row 1, column 1 and row 2, column 2 could explain that pattern.

Both examples use two changes. The difference is how those changes are distributed. Neither possible history is uniquely proved by the receiver's checks.
P3.completion_evidence: Tutor clearly contrasts both observed check patterns and the corresponding possible same-row vs distributed two-bit explanations, without claiming unique inference.

P3.source_instructional_action: Contrast the two complete valid originals and distinct one- versus three-flip histories ending in the exact same received grid; distinguish teacher comparison from receiver evidence.
P3.exact_delivery:
These two histories begin with different valid grids but end with the same received bits.

In the first, changing row 2, column 1 gives the received grid—one change. In the second, changing row 1, columns 1 and 2, plus row 2, column 2 gives that same received grid—three changes.

Both make only row 2 and column 1 fail. The instructor can compare both constructed histories; the receiver sees just the same final grid and checks. So correcting as if exactly one error occurred may be wrong.
P3.completion_evidence: Tutor contrasts both different valid originals, exact changes and identical complete received bits/check results, and correctly limits any single-error correction claim.

P3.source_instructional_action: Contrast detected three-bit corruption with the undetected four-corner rectangle, explaining differing group flip counts and received evidence rather than counting errors alone.
P3.exact_delivery:
Compare two multi-bit histories.

The three-change example leaves row 2 and column 1 failing, so the receiver detects a parity violation.

In the four-corner rectangle, row 1 and row 2 each contain two changes, and columns 1 and 2 also contain two. All seven checks pass, so that corruption goes undetected.

The difference is not simply three changes versus four. It's how many changed positions belong to each complete row and column. Some multi-bit patterns are detected; others are not.
P3.completion_evidence: Tutor contrasts the verified detected three-flip outcome with all-pass rectangle, explains check-group distribution and avoids overgeneralizing about all multi-bit errors.

P3.source_instructional_action: Contrast warranted and unwarranted statements from three kinds of receiver evidence, explicitly separating detection, possible location and conditional correction.
P3.exact_delivery:
Compare what the receiver can say with what it cannot prove.

A failed check shows a broken parity rule. It does not reveal the original bits or uniquely count the errors. When one row and one column fail, their intersection is a candidate under a one-error assumption—not proof.

And when all seven checks pass, the receiver knows only that the rules are satisfied. The rectangle shows why that cannot guarantee unchanged data.

Detection is not the same as locating every error, and a proposed correction is justified only when its assumptions are supported.
P3.completion_evidence: Tutor explicitly contrasts justified versus unjustified claims for failed checks, conditional intersection and all-pass results, distinguishing detection/localization/correction and evidence limits.
